name: PIVCO-Huffman (pivco-huffman)
baseline: huf0 (zstd's Huffman decoder from FiniteStateEntropy, X1 single-symbol and X2 double-symbol variants) and an in-tree traditional 4-stream table Huffman decoder; Oodle Huffman (oo-huff) is wired into bench/bench_fair.c only when an Oodle SDK is linked and does not appear in the BENCHMARKS.md tables
workload: Decode of a 4M-symbol Huffman-coded block sequence repeated 100 times (400M symbols per run), 5 runs, median of 3 best; synthetic distributions (proba80, flat, zipfian, ...) and real files (html_wiki, english, json_api, source_c, ...).
claimed_speedup: Apple M4 Max: proba80 15,339 MB/s vs huf0 X2 2,617 (5.91x best-of-others); real text 4.3-4.8 GB/s, 2.0-2.5x huf0_x2; Xeon 6975P-C AVX-512: english 7,909 vs huf0 X2 1,875 (4.22x), html_wiki 4,765 (2.96x), proba80 22,581 (11.70x). Encoded size within 1-4% of traditional Huffman.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5.0 on Amazon Linux 2023 for the Xeon 6975P-C (c8i) and Graviton 4 (c8g) tables, clang-20 for the AMD EPYC 7R13 Zen 3 (c6a) table; CMakeLists.txt adds -Wall -Wextra -O3 and, on AVX-512 hosts, -mavx512f -mavx512bw -mavx512vl -mavx512vbmi -mavx512vbmi2 -mavx512vpopcntdq -mavx2 -mbmi2 -msse4.1 -mpopcnt (AVX2 hosts: -mavx2 -mbmi2 -msse4.1 -mpopcnt); Apple M4 compiler not stated
hardware: Apple M4 Max (NEON, block 8192); Intel Xeon 6975P-C AVX-512 VBMI2 (AWS c8i, 2 vCPU); AWS Graviton 4 Neoverse V2 (c8g.large, taskset -c 0); AMD EPYC 7R13 Zen 3 AVX2/SSE4.1 (AWS c6a, 2 vCPU, block 4096)
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in: new bitstream (PivCo partition bitmaps), block-based (4096-8192 symbol blocks), encoder walks the Huffman tree; needs SIMD with permute/compress primitives (NEON, AVX-512 VBMI2, AVX2). Encoded size 1-4% above traditional Huffman. PHA variant adds FSE/ANS coded bitmaps for better ratio on skewed data at lower decode speed.
caveats: README marks the project as WIP and not production-ready; co-authored with an AI assistant per commit trailers. BENCHMARKS.md is a 2026-05-15 snapshot marked 'Last content review: NEVER'. On Zen 3 (SSE/AVX2) html_wiki, json_api and log_apache lose to huf0 X2 at 0.94-0.95x and several rows are only 1.06-1.3x; Graviton 4 real text is 1.29-1.47x. flat_M7 on M4 is only 1.43x. The README TL;DR's real-text range (4.3-4.8 GB/s, 2.0-2.5x) does not include the M4 table's english row (6142 MB/s, 2.55x). In-memory decode-only microbenchmark; huf0 uses 128 KB chunks while PIVCO uses 4096-8192-symbol blocks; tables use the --no-fse (PH) configuration. Paper (PDF on github.io) and arXiv copy not opened (hosts blocked).

tradeoffs: FSE is a table-based tANS coder (precise like arithmetic coding, but slower than Huff0); Huff0 is Huffman with 4-stream interleaving, loses ratio on skewed distributions (cannot go below 1 bit per symbol). Both are block-oriented with a header describing the distribution.

name: FSST (Fast Static Symbol Table)
workload: Compression of short strings (22 'dbtext' data sets, each an 8 MB file, single-threaded) with random access per string; LZ4 used in file-based mode.
claimed_speedup: PVLDB 2020 paper Table 1 (22 dbtext sets, 8 MB files, single thread): FSST compression speed beats LZ4 on 21 of 22 sets (e.g. genome 1,307 vs 566 MB/s, uuid 1,113 vs 632, credentials 984 vs 439; LZ4 wins on hex 1,097 vs 944) with a higher compression factor on 21 of 22 (e.g. genome 3.32 vs 1.59, uuid 2.44 vs 1.55; LZ4 wins on urls 2.77 vs 2.16); paper text gives average factor 2.28x vs LZ4 1.70x. Decompression speed is mixed: FSST faster on 12 sets (e.g. genome 2,838 vs 1,126 MB/s, c_name 3,519 vs 2,960), LZ4 faster on 10 (e.g. hex 1,891 vs 1,546, email 2,388 vs 1,547) (counts derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Strings only (symbol table of up to 8-byte symbols mapped to 1-byte codes); static table per block, random access to single strings without block decode; not a general-purpose byte-stream compressor. Best on short-string columns, ratio gain largest on machine-generated IDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (PVLDB vol 13 no 12, 2020); numbers read from the paper PDF checked into the repo (via raw.githubusercontent.com). LZ4 version is old (1.8.1) with g++ 8.3.1. Decompression is on par with LZ4, slower on 10 of 22 sets; the main win is compression ratio, compression speed and per-string random access. File mode is LZ4's best case per the paper. Replication package (paper/ directory with dbtext corpus and Makefile) is in the repo; it needs Linux perf counters and LZ4 1.8.1 on PATH.

name: Rapidgzip
baseline: GNU gzip (single-threaded deflate decoder); also compared with pigz, igzip (ISA-L), bgzip and pzstd
workload: Decompression of arbitrary gzip files (Silesia tar repeated 20x, 3.95 GiB; 4 GiB base64 data) on a Ryzen 3900X, plus scaling to 128 cores on 2x EPYC 7702.
claimed_speedup: Ryzen 3900X, 20x-silesia with existing index: 5640 MB/s (0 threads=auto) vs gzip 293 MB/s (18.8x); from scratch 2070 MB/s (6.9x); 4GiB-base64 from scratch 5060 MB/s vs gzip 250 MB/s (20.1x). README: up to 24 GB/s with index and 12 GB/s without on 128 cores; 24.3 GB/s vs 9.5 GB/s for pzstd with index. Paper abstract: 5.6 GB/s on Silesia, speedup 33 over GNU gzip, with 128 cores. README: single-core decompression close to igzip and about twice as fast as bgzip (zlib).
license: Apache-2.0 AND MIT (repo page lists both; per-file split not checked)
tradeoffs: Multi-core only wins: single-thread speed is close to igzip, not faster. Needs memory for chunk cache and a two-stage decode of unknown windows; with an index it reaches higher bandwidth. Read-only decompressor (compression is delegated to other tools). C++17, usable as header-only C++ library.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (ACM HPDC 2023, DOI 10.1145/3588195.3592992); the paper PDF in mxmlnkn/indexed_bzip2/results/paper was opened, but neither it nor the README states the compiler or flags. The headline gain is parallel scaling versus single-threaded GNU gzip, not a faster single-thread inflate: in the paper (rapidgzip 0.5.0), single-threaded rapidgzip reached 153 MB/s, while bgzip was 1.9x and igzip 4.3x as fast; the README's claim that single-core speed is close to igzip refers to later versions. Baseline is GNU gzip rather than zlib. The README scaling plots used rapidgzip 0.9.0, and its values are higher than the paper's. The paper's text gives GNU gzip on Silesia as "172 GB/s", an evident typo for MB/s.

claimed_speedup: Suite 2026-09-21 (8.7 GB corpus of logs, JSON events, SQL dumps, Parquet), one thread, MB/s: Glyd --max ratio 3.98 decompresses 1,571 vs zstd -3 (ratio 3.86) 1,425 on Graviton3 (1.10x) but 1,287 vs 1,518 on Sapphire Rapids (0.85x, slower), and compresses at 233 vs 313 and 266 vs 377. Glyd default (ratio 2.82) decompresses 3,309 on Graviton3 and 2,752 on Sapphire Rapids vs LZ4 (ratio 2.72) 1,394 and 1,206, compressing at 332 vs 504 and 327 vs 456. Eight threads: Glyd default decompresses 22,707 MB/s and --max 10,413 vs zstd -3 1,422 and LZ4 1,392, but zstd and LZ4 frames are decoded on one thread. README summary: reads 3-7x faster than zstd on a server, writes at 0.71-0.77x zstd -3's speed.
license: BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0 (codec); BUSL-1.1 (glyd-store and GPU parts)
tradeoffs: Codec is dual-licensed but the store and GPU components are under Business Source License 1.1 (commercial use needs a license). Output decodes in parallel, so multicore reads are far faster than zstd/LZ4 frames that decode on one thread. Compresses slower than LZ4 and zstd -3 at the same levels; record mode costs 2-2.7x the CPU of zstd. Rust crate with C ABI callable from C++.
caveats: First party, very young repo (240 stars, 1 fork) with sweeping claims. Like-for-like (one thread, similar ratio) the decode win over zstd -3 is small and platform-dependent: 1.10x on Graviton3, 0.85x (slower) on Sapphire Rapids, and compression is slower than zstd -3 on both. The 22.7 GB/s headline compares 8-thread Glyd decoding with single-thread zstd/LZ4 frame decoding. The LZ4 baseline in examples/bench_suite.rs uses the lz4 crate's streaming frame Decoder with read_to_end, not the LZ4 block API, which likely explains LZ4 decoding at only about 1.4 GB/s; the README's 'each codec on its fastest API' does not hold for LZ4, so the LZ4 decode comparison is weak. Glyd writes a per-block checksum; zstd frames here carry none. Store and GPU parts are BUSL-1.1 (non-commercial free).

Gains on structured formats need a format description or training; on CSV compression speed is capped near 64 MB/s by parsing (snippet). lzbench lists openzl as a target but its README table has no openzl rows.

name: FastPFor (SIMD-FastPFOR, SIMD-BP128)
baseline: Simple-8b and VByte (varint); also scalar FastPFOR/SimplePFOR
workload: Decoding sorted/small 32-bit integer lists (posting lists, delta coded) in blocks of 128+ integers with SSE SIMD, measured in billions of integers per second.
claimed_speedup: Paper (as quoted in search-result snippets, not opened): SIMD-FastPFOR within 10% of Simple-8b compression ratio while about 2x faster to decode; SIMD-BP128 more than 3x faster to decode than Simple-8b; SIMD schemes 2-3x faster than scalar FastPFOR and varint. stars_or_usage: 978 stars; used in zsearch, GMAP/GSNAP; Lucene 4.6 format referenced; ports to Java, C#, Go
tradeoffs: SIMD codecs need SSE2/SSSE3 (ARM64 NEON supported); best throughput on 128-integer blocks of 32-bit values; SIMD-FastPFOR trades some speed for 5-15% better ratio than SIMD-BP128; varint-G8IU in the library is patented.
caveats: The repo README claims are against gzip/LZO/Snappy/LZ4 (not in the baseline list). The Simple-8b and VByte comparison is derived from a competitor's (TurboPFor) README table dated 2019.11; the linked issue #47 names Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz and gcc 9.2 but no compiler flags.
